client: Lately, family gatherings have been really hard for me since my grandma passed away last month. I keep expecting to see her there, and when she’s not, it feels like this huge emptiness that I can’t shake. I’m not sure if therapy can help with something like this—it just feels like this loss is always going to hurt.
therapist: It sounds like the absence of your grandma is deeply felt, especially in those familiar family moments—that sense of emptiness can be so heavy. It’s okay for grief to linger, but let’s explore how those expectations of seeing her might be shaping your experience. What thoughts come up for you when you notice she’s not there?

client: When I notice she’s not there, I just think, "This isn’t right, she should be here." It feels like the family isn’t complete anymore, and it’s hard to enjoy anything because it’s overshadowed by her absence. I don’t know how to move past that feeling—it’s like I’m stuck in this loop of missing her.
therapist: That sense of things not being right without her must feel so jarring, especially when the family dynamic feels incomplete. It’s natural to feel stuck in that loop of missing her, but I wonder if we could gently explore how her absence also coexists with the love and memories she left behind. What’s one memory of her that brings you comfort, even if it’s bittersweet?

client: I remember how she used to bake these special cookies for holidays—she had this way of making everyone feel so loved and included. It’s bittersweet because it makes me smile, but then I feel this ache knowing she won’t do it again. I don’t know if focusing on memories helps, though—it just reminds me of what I’ve lost.
therapist: It sounds like those memories of her baking bring warmth but also a deep ache—those mixed feelings can be so tender and painful all at once. It’s okay to feel both the joy and the loss, but I wonder if we could explore how those memories might still hold space for her in a way that feels meaningful, even if it’s hard. How does it feel when you think about carrying forward her tradition of making others feel loved and included?

client: I guess the idea of carrying forward her tradition feels nice in theory, but it also feels overwhelming. I’m not sure I can do it the way she did—she had this way of making everything feel so effortless and special. It’s hard to imagine stepping into that role without feeling like I’m just failing to live up to her memory.
therapist: It sounds like the idea of continuing her tradition brings both warmth and a lot of pressure—like her way of doing things feels impossible to match. It’s okay to feel overwhelmed, and it doesn’t mean you have to do it exactly as she did. What if we explored how you could make this tradition your own, in a way that feels authentic to you? How might that look?

client: I never really thought about making it my own—I always saw it as her thing that I couldn’t live up to. But maybe I could try something simpler, like just writing little notes to family members the way she always remembered everyone’s favorite things. It still feels scary though—what if it just makes everyone miss her more?
therapist: That sounds like a thoughtful and meaningful way to honor her memory, even if it feels a little scary. It’s natural to worry about how others might react, but those little notes could also bring warmth and connection in a way that feels true to her spirit. What do you think might help you feel more comfortable taking that first step?

client: I think starting small might help—maybe just writing one note instead of trying to do something big. But I’m still worried it’ll feel forced or that I’ll be comparing myself to her the whole time. It’s hard to imagine doing this without feeling like I’m not measuring up to her legacy.
therapist: Starting small is such a wise approach—it gives you space to ease into this without the pressure of perfection. It makes sense that comparison creeps in, but remember, this isn’t about replacing her; it’s about letting her kindness inspire yours in a way that feels genuine to you. What would it feel like to focus on the intention behind the note—the love you’re sharing—rather than measuring it against her legacy?

client: Focusing on the intention feels like it takes some of the pressure off—it’s not about being perfect or living up to her, but just sharing love in my own way. Still, it’s hard to shake the fear that it won’t feel the same or that I’ll disappoint people who are missing her. What if it just reminds everyone of what’s gone?
therapist: It sounds like you’re starting to find a gentler way to approach this, which is a big step—shifting the focus to intention can ease some of that pressure. It’s understandable to worry about how others might feel, but love shared in your own way can still be deeply meaningful, even if it’s different from hers. What do you think might help you let go of the fear of disappointing others and trust that your efforts will be enough?

client: I think reminding myself that it’s okay to do things differently might help—it doesn’t have to be perfect or just like her. But I still worry that my efforts won’t feel like enough, especially when everyone’s grieving too. It’s hard to trust that people will appreciate it, even if it’s not what they’re used to.
therapist: It sounds like you’re starting to find a gentler, more forgiving approach—acknowledging that it’s okay to do things differently is such an important step. It’s natural to worry about how others will receive it, especially when everyone’s grieving, but your efforts don’t have to be perfect to be meaningful. What might it feel like to trust that your love and thoughtfulness are enough, even if it’s not exactly what they’re used to?

client: Trusting that my love and thoughtfulness are enough feels really hard—I’m so used to comparing myself to her and feeling like I fall short. But maybe it’s worth trying, even if it doesn’t feel perfect, because at least it’s something to keep her spirit alive in my own way. I just don’t know how to quiet that voice in my head that says it’s not good enough.
therapist: It sounds like that voice of comparison is really persistent, making it hard to trust your own efforts—that’s such a heavy feeling to carry. But it’s so powerful that you’re considering trying anyway, even if it doesn’t feel perfect, because keeping her spirit alive in your own way matters. What might it look like to gently challenge that voice when it says, “It’s not good enough”?

client: Challenging that voice feels really hard—it’s been there for so long, and it feels like it’s rooted in truth sometimes. I guess I could try to remind myself that my grandma would probably want me to do things my way, not try to copy her, but it’s still hard to believe that my way is enough. What if I just end up feeling worse about it?
therapist: It sounds like that voice feels deeply ingrained, and questioning it can feel shaky when it’s been such a constant presence. It’s such a powerful thought, though, that your grandma would likely want you to do things your way—not as a copy, but as an extension of her love through you. What might it feel like to take small steps, like writing a note, and then gently reflect on how it felt, rather than focusing on whether it was “enough”?
